options.text: Hear and acknowledge the stop
Leave the contest under control
Confirm the restart cue

Continue the old loose-puck plan
Assume YOU own the restart

questions.prompt: Why can the right decision change even when nobody touches the puck?
questions.explanation: The coach changed the task and the restart conditions. A player must follow the new instruction, then re-read possession, pressure, and support.

options.text: D1
YOU
C

questions.explanation: The puck is assigned to D1, so this question is about support without possession.

questions.prompt: Which two changes might make your support more useful?

options.text: Stay hidden behind Gold 1 until the pass arrives
Show a ready stick after scanning
Adjust the receiving angle

questions.explanation: Moving and preparing can help D1 see an option; any new location still needs a lane check.

questions.prompt: Arrange a way to reoffer along this wall.

options.text: Identify Gold 1’s blocking position
Move to change the passing angle
Look back and prepare to receive

questions.explanation: The order is a suggested support routine rather than a fixed skating pattern.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a different receiving angle from D1.
questions.explanation: Coming off the boards can separate the passing route from Gold 1. Check C’s space rather than crowding it.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 follows your inward move, which response could help?

options.text: Call for a pass without looking at Gold 1
Reoffer elsewhere or make room for C
Remain still because your first move should have worked

questions.explanation: A supporter should update the option; the first movement does not guarantee availability.

questions.prompt: How can your movement help D1 even if D1 passes to C?
questions.explanation: Explain how moving Gold 1 or clearing a route can help another teammate. Receiving the puck is not the only useful outcome.

questions.prompt: What is the direct route Gold 1 is occupying?

options.text: The lane between D1 and YOU
The route from C to Navy’s net
The far blue-line exit

questions.explanation: Gold 1 sits between D1 and YOU, so moving off that line can reoffer support; if Gold 1 follows, the new lane must be read.

questions.prompt: Which two calls help D1 use your movement?

options.text: Say when you are clear of the shadow
Identify C’s inside support
Call “I’m open” and leave D1 to guess your new angle

questions.explanation: D1 needs your new availability and C’s inside relationship to choose; a one-word call gives no geometry.

questions.prompt: Move YOU inward from the boards to create a visible angle for D1.
questions.explanation: The inward angle steps off Gold 1’s direct route and gives D1 a short option; if Gold 1 follows, C may become the next outlet.

questions.prompt: How can movement help D1 even if the puck goes to C?
questions.explanation: Stepping off the direct lane can pull Gold 1 and open C or D1’s next route; if the defender ignores you, D1 can use the space you created.

questions.prompt: What support job is explicitly assigned to YOU?

options.text: Wait at the far blue line
Pressure W as an opponent
Offer a short inside outlet

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns a short inside outlet, rather than an immediate stretch.

questions.prompt: Which two features would suit that outlet?

options.text: Enough separation from Gold 1
A route W can actually see
The greatest possible distance from W

questions.explanation: Short support needs usable spacing and a route, not just proximity.

questions.prompt: Order a support response to W’s pressure.

options.text: Read Gold 1’s approach
Move closer to Navy’s net and inside W
Prepare for a pass or another change

questions.explanation: Keep updating pressure while moving; the routine is not a rigid play call.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to Navy’s net than W to suggest a short inside option.
questions.explanation: A position closer to Navy’s net and inside W can offer a release while avoiding the same wall pressure. Several spots may work.

questions.prompt: If W escapes Gold 1 with secure possession, what changes?

options.text: You may move forward while remaining available
You must remain underneath for the rest of the shift
You should stop watching the puck

questions.explanation: The support distance can expand when the carrier has time; possession quality still matters.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between supporting W and skating into W’s problem?
questions.explanation: A useful option creates a different angle or time advantage instead of joining the same pressure.

questions.prompt: Which Navy teammate offers a deeper reset behind YOU if W remains pinned?

options.text: D1
Gold 1
Gold 2

questions.explanation: D1 is the deeper Navy option behind YOU, so W can have a connected reset if Gold 1 keeps pressure on the wall; if D1 is covered, hold a support angle instead of forcing the pass.

questions.prompt: Which two cues tell YOU whether to stay underneath W?

options.text: Gold 1’s pressure on W
W’s puck control
D1’s old position alone

questions.explanation: Pressure and control determine whether W needs a close outlet; D1’s old spot cannot answer the immediate support question.

questions.prompt: Move YOU below and inside W to present the assigned short outlet.
questions.explanation: The lower-inside spot gives W a short lane away from Gold 1; if W gains space, widen to support the next play.

questions.prompt: What would make you leave the short-outlet position?
questions.explanation: Leave when W has secure control and a better visible lane opens, or when pressure closes your route; if W remains pinned, stay available.

after.title: Offer a short inside outlet
after.objective: Offer a short inside outlet for a teammate under pressure.
after.briefing: Navy W owns the puck in a wide lane, with Gold 1 nearby. YOU start farther up ice and nearer the middle. In this exercise, offer a short inside outlet closer to Navy’s defended left net than W, if the lane is usable.
cues: The coach assigns a short inside outlet.
W is the navy puck carrier under nearby gold pressure.
